content.text: When unstable nuclei decay, they change into different nuclei. Nuclear equations describe these changes, showing what happens to protons and neutrons. Understanding nuclear equations helps us predict the products of radioactive decay and track how elements transform.

In every nuclear equation, both the total mass number (nucleon number) and the total atomic number (proton number/charge) must balance on both sides. This reflects the conservation of nucleons and charge.
Total mass number before = total mass number after
Total atomic number before = total atomic number after
Both superscripts (mass numbers) must balance. Both subscripts (atomic numbers) must balance.

To check your nuclear equation is correct, add up all the mass numbers (top numbers) on each side -- they must be equal. Then add up all the atomic numbers (bottom numbers) on each side -- they must also be equal. If they do not balance, look for errors in the products.
"The electron in beta decay comes from the shells"
— The beta particle comes from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton.
— Gamma emission releases energy but doesn't change mass number or atomic number.
— Mass number is the count of nucleons. Actual mass is measured in atomic mass units or kilograms.
"All radioactive decay produces a different element"
— Gamma decay doesn't. Alpha and beta decay do change the element.
— Many nuclei undergo decay chains with multiple types of decay.

Alpha decay: mass number drops by 4, atomic number drops by 2. Beta decay: mass number stays the same, atomic number increases by 1. Gamma emission: no change to mass number or atomic number.

After alpha or beta decay, the daughter nucleus is often left in an excited energy state. The nucleus then releases excess energy as a gamma ray to reach its ground state. Gamma emission does not change A or Z.
